meaning.evidence: Almost all the original text is left in place, so the points survive, but some swaps change things: "eight quid every Saturday night" changes the currency, and the money passage becomes inconsistent: "sixty cents on any quid ... a quid is worth one hundred and six cents ... he never spends the dollar". "I am scared stiff" overstates "I am afraid".

sense.evidence: Several wrong-sense swaps: "scared stiff" for the polite "I am afraid"; "It is all with the bloke" for "It is all with the man" (the man as the individual); "the old bloke" for "the old man" (father); "a beaut business man" for a good (sound) businessman; "very, dead careful".

authenticity.evidence: Words are swapped into otherwise untouched 1900s prose: "making a mug of yourself in the way that some of these young blokes who haven't had to work for it do"; "Bloody hell, I simply mention these things" is bolted on; "a bloody good deal like feeding his weight in corn".

register.evidence: Lighter than level 3 overall: long stretches are the original word for word ("Naturally, that is the time when knowing whether the pie comes before the ice-cream, and how to run an automobile isn't going to be of any real use to you."), with token swaps like "bloke", "quid", "uni". Swearing within vulgarity 1.

tone.evidence: The dry fatherly reproof mostly survives because the original is mostly kept, but "Bloody hell, I simply mention these things" and "scared stiff" make the old man sound flustered rather than wry.

flow.evidence: Clunky joins: "very, dead careful", "a bloody good deal like feeding his weight in corn to a scalawag steer", "Bloody hell, I simply mention".

variety.evidence: Leans on "bloke" (used about a dozen times, replacing man, fellow and traveling man alike: "the first travelling bloke") and "beaut" twice.

essence.evidence: Recognisably the letter because the text is largely untouched; the aphorisms ("plenty of room at the top here, but there is no lift in the building") survive.

problems.why: Broken construction; 'dead' cannot replace the second 'very' here.

problems.quote: Bloody hell, I simply mention these things because I am scared stiff
problems.original: I simply mention these things because I am afraid
problems.why: Bolted-on oath, and 'scared stiff' takes 'afraid' in the wrong sense (polite regret, not fear).

problems.quote: sixty cents on any quid that comes to him. But a quid is worth one hundred and six cents to a beaut business man, and he never spends the dollar
problems.original: sixty cents on any dollar that comes to him. But a dollar is worth one hundred and six cents to a good business man, and he never spends the dollar
problems.why: Currency swap leaves quids, cents and dollars mixed in one argument.

problems.quote: It is all with the bloke.
problems.original: It is all with the man.
problems.why: Mechanical 'man' to 'bloke' swap reads oddly in an aphorism.
'Traveling man' is a commercial traveller; 'bloke' loses the sense.

problems.quote: a bloody good deal like feeding his weight in corn
problems.original: a good deal like feeding his weight in corn
problems.why: Oath inserted where it attaches to the wrong phrase.

A.summary: Largely the original with mechanical word swaps; several wrong-sense substitutions, a broken phrase and mixed currency, and well under the level asked.

meaning.evidence: Every point survives in order: Cambridge, the steer, the mailing-desk, no lift, licking stamps, the talent in a napkin, sixty cents on the dollar, Munchausen. Swapping dollars for "eight quid" and "any quid" shifts the setting and leaves "a quid's worth a hundred and six cents" mixed.

sense.evidence: Terms fit well: "a no-hoper steer" for scalawag, "your native nous" for common-sense, "rolling in it and can wear it", "telling porkies", "my commercial travellers' bills" for drummers' bills, "the drapery game" for dry-goods.

authenticity.evidence: Natural: "it fair makes a bloke go round-shouldered", "I haven't seen a skerrick of you taking honours", "don't go getting it into your noggin". Reads like an Australian father writing.

register.evidence: Middling Aussie throughout, a real retelling without becoming a yarn; one "bloody bad business" within vulgarity 1. On brief for level 3.

tone.evidence: The wry, stern fatherly letter comes through: "There's heaps of room at the top here, but there's no lift in the building."

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly: "Give some fellas a talent wrapped in a napkin to start in business with, and they'd swap the talent for a dud gold brick and lose the napkin too".

variety.evidence: Varied: "skerrick", "nous", "noggin", "no-hoper", "porkies", "drapery game"; "bloke" and "cos" recur a fair bit ("cos I trusted", "just cos I've sat tight", "cos he won't wear it", "cos I'm afraid").

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the Self-Made Merchant's letter, with its homely business aphorisms intact.

problems.quote: with eight quid every Saturday night
problems.original: with eight dollars every Saturday night
problems.why: Changes the currency of a Chicago letter; then leaves 'cents' beside 'quid'.

problems.quote: But a quid's worth a hundred and six cents
problems.original: But a dollar is worth one hundred and six cents
problems.why: Quid with cents is a mixed unit.

problems.quote: cos he won't wear it once you've left uni
problems.original: because he won't stand it after you leave college
problems.why: 'Cos' repeated four times becomes a tic.

B.summary: A natural, well-judged level-3 Aussie retelling that keeps every point and the father's wry voice; minor currency mix.

meaning.evidence: Every point survives and the dollars are kept ("eight dollars every Saturday night", "sixty cents out of any dollar"). One line is garbled: "feeding a mongrel steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn" makes it sound as if the steer won't fatten its weight.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "making a galah of yourself", "the old man's loaded and can wear it", "send you broke", "telling porkies", "my reps' bills". "a mongrel steer" for scalawag is close enough.

authenticity.evidence: Natural: "I've kept me mouth shut", "won't be a scrap of real use to you", "sweet-talk the other bloke's talent into it". Some US forms kept ("once you're out of college", "out East"), defensible in a Chicago letter.

register.evidence: Level 3 is met: a real retelling with "galah", "porkies", "loaded", without becoming a yarn; no swearing, which vulgarity 1 allows. Slightly lighter than it could be.

tone.evidence: The stern but affectionate father comes through: "I can give you a start, but after that you'll have to blast your own way to the front."

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly except the steer sentence: "feeding a mongrel steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn".

variety.evidence: Varied: "galah", "loaded", "banking on", "a scrap of", "sweet-talk", "porkies", "reps"; nothing leaned on.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original letter, aphorisms intact: "There's plenty of room at the top here, but there's no lift in the building."

problems.quote: feeding a mongrel steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn
problems.original: feeding his weight in corn to a scalawag steer that won't fat up
problems.why: Word order garbles the image; it should be feeding the steer its own weight in corn.
Keeps the American 'college' where uni would be the Aussie choice; defensible in context.

C.summary: A natural, faithful level-3 retelling that keeps the dollars and the father's voice; one garbled simile.
